title: C#
subtitle: The Windows side of my Teams integration is C# on .NET 8: a media service on Microsoft's real-time SDK, screen-share publication, and a product MCP server later ported to the official .NET SDK.

stats.label: lines of .NET 8 in the media service's six-project solution
call-to-persona bindings exercised by its unit suite
lines in the weather MCP server, ported to the official C# SDK

lede: Helix had to put a self-hosted voice agent into Microsoft Teams calls, and Microsoft's real-time media stack runs only on Windows. The service is .NET 8, a six-project solution covering host, calls, media, transport, contracts and unit tests, built on Microsoft's real-time media SDK and hosted on an Azure virtual machine with managed identity and vault-held secrets. It handles the calling callbacks and call lifecycle, answers inbound calls and places outbound ones, and binds each call to a persona. The identity side is told in Solving the digital-employee identity. Media callbacks copy the frame and return immediately, so SDK threads never wait on the network.
quote: I keep the Windows component narrow so the system's logic stays in one place.
evidence: Microsoft Teams real-time media: a narrow .NET 8 media bridge of 6,400 lines on Microsoft's real-time media SDK that joins calls and moves frames, with all conversation state left in the Linux engine.
Native interop in C#: media callbacks that copy and return at once, unmanaged audio buffers released outside the garbage collector, and a byte-identical binary protocol shared with Rust.
MCP server design: a weather MCP server of 9,650 lines ported from TypeScript to the official C# SDK with the ASP.NET Core HTTP transport.
author: Corey James
